title: Bangladesh Malaysia FTA could redraw $219 mn apparel trade
content:
Bangladesh-Malaysia FTA talks closed their first round, with no textile tariff cuts agreed and completion targeted by end-2027.
Bangladesh’s RMG exports to Malaysia rose 15.35 per cent to $218.59 million in FY2025-26 as woven garments surged.
Rules of origin, D-8 PTA preferences and Indian and Chinese supplier dominance will decide gains in synthetics, nonwovens and technical textiles.

title: Bangladesh selects 100 factories for $3 bn Japan apparel push
content:
Bangladesh’s $3 billion Japan apparel ambition faces a product test after supplying 5.63 per cent of Japan’s garment imports in 2025.
TexPro shows China’s share falling, but Vietnam and Cambodia gained faster; its Japan-bound garments fell 4.67 per cent in January-August 2026.
Outerwear gained, but T-shirts, trousers and knit pullovers weakened; the EPA offers steadier access, not a windfall.

title: Four yarn moves, €30 mn flax project: Is specialisation gaining
content:
US, Portugal and India/UK textile moves in August–October 2026 highlight investment in specialised filament, fibre processing, technology and engineering. 
Reshoring Textiles, Parkdale and Basant Fibertek acquisition prices were undisclosed; Nafilux plans €30 million (~$33.3 million) and 250 jobs.
ITMF reported weak spinning and finishing conditions; the deals do not establish a wider sourcing shift.

title: Polyester filament yarn: Why the cost push is losing steam?
content:
Polyester filament yarn prices in China and India slipped in the week to October 30, despite higher naphtha, MEG and PTA costs.
China’s POY 150D/96F fell 0.85 per cent, DTY 48D/36F eased 0.74 per cent, while India’s FDY 68D/24F lost 0.72 per cent.
Weaving and texturising buyers bought only for immediate needs, limiting producers’ ability to pass on feedstock increases.

title: North India’s cotton yarn steady as traders await demand revival
content:
North Indian cotton yarn prices stayed steady as sluggish weaving and knitting demand and payment constraints kept Ludhiana and Delhi trading subdued.
Panipat’s recycled yarn market remained weak despite festivities, with home textiles hit by slow payments and uncertain exports.
Cotton fell ₹40–50 (~$0.42–0.53) per maund on weak mill demand, softer ICE futures; seed cotton rose on ginning mill purchases.

title: India’s polyester raw material prices mixed, PSF & filament yarn rise
content:
India’s polyester market diverged last week as domestic feedstock stayed subdued while PSF and filament yarn rose by ₹2 (~$0.02) per kg.
RIL held PTA steady, cut MEG to ₹71 per kg and eased polyester melt; Bhilosa raised POY, FDY and PTY by ₹2 per kg.
Chinese PTA and MEG quotations strengthened to $1,015 and $720 per tonne by October 30, signalling upward pressure in Asian polyester feedstock markets.

title: Bangladesh forms wage board to review garment workers' pay
content:
Bangladesh formed a six-member wage board to review garment workers’ minimum pay amid protests demanding Tk 30,000 (~$240) per month. 
The panel, comprising employer, worker and independent representatives, will recommend a revised wage structure. 
The current minimum wage is Tk 12,500, while recent labour law amendments reduced the wage review cycle from five years to three.

title: Indian exporters gearing up for a bigger European play?
content:
Indian apparel exporters are positioning for a tariff advantage in Europe as the India-EU FTA moves towards possible signing in December 2026, with implementation expected by spring 2027.
Gokaldas Exports sees Europe’s export share rising to 25–30 per cent in three to five years, while Raymond Lifestyle targets 20–25 per cent.
EU sustainability and traceability rules will shape lasting gains.

title: How can Bangladesh apparel exporters reduce payment risks?
content:
Bangladesh garment exporters face renewed payment-risk concerns after BKMEA reportedly warned members about more than a dozen entities.
Six factories’ seven complaints involved about $2.34 million, citing unpaid bills, delivery failures, shipment delays and alleged contractual violations.
The cases underline the need for due diligence, clear contracts and bank-backed, lawful payment safeguards.
